Summary (auto): short technical deep dive on burst policies, queueing model tradeoffs, and practical KV cache warmup strategies for cached and quantized serving inside a VPC/on-prem deployment. Focus on reserved GPU sizing and burst window safety nets.

Topics: burst modelling, queueing (M/G/1-ish discussion), prewarmed pools, KV cache hit-rate warmup, quantization latency delta, network egress in VPC, dedicated vs hosted fallback policies.

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Maya Chen: Okay everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, this is Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Diego and Priya are with me today from the solutions team. How's Lyra doing?
[00:00:12] Samir Patel: Good, Maya. Thanks. We wanted a deep dive on capacity — we've been seeing spikes that blow past our reserved throughput, and the autoscaler hasn't been friendly.
[00:00:22] Diego Alvarez: Right, and we asked for the trace so we could run it through our burst simulator. Quick note — apologies if transcription is a bit rough, I talk fast.
[00:00:30] Joan Kim: No worries. We'll jump into the queueing stuff. But first, a quick run-down of what we care about: 99th latency under 800ms, cost per 1k requests under $X, and of course data never leaves our VPC.
[00:00:45] Priya Rao: Great. We'll frame the convo around three pillars: (1) what's causing the burst surface area, (2) how KV cache warmup changes effective token cost/latency, and (3) reserved GPU sizing and fallback safety nets.

[00:01:05] Diego: To start, two common burst patterns we've seen — steady-state traffic with rare high-concurrency fanout (user-triggered batch jobs) and diurnal-thresholded microbursts driven by downstream lambda-style functions. For modelling we often switch from a pure Poisson assumption to a compound process — a background M/M/1-like stream plus periodic compound arrivals.
[00:01:34] Elliot Graves: Can you expand on compound? Like, how to parameterize?
[00:01:37] Diego: Yeah, so think of a baseline RPS lambda, then a separate 'session' arrival that emits N correlated requests within T seconds. Parameterize session size distribution (heavy tail), inter-arrival between sessions, and correlation with prompt length. That's critical; big prompts can saturate KV cache and increase GPU memory pressure.
[00:01:58] Samir: Our big problem is warmup; after idle periods we see the KV hit rate collapse and latency jumps up to 3x for the first hundred requests. Any practical mitigations?
[00:02:12] Priya: We've implemented a few heuristics. One is prewarming kv cache for hot prefixes — keep some preserved cache shards in prewarmed pools so that when traffic arrives, the majority of token keys are already present. Another is a short-lived aggressive billing-friendly prewarm: spin up micro-pools on burst detection and route traffic through them for first N seconds.
[00:02:36] Joan: Micro-pools — does that mean additional reserved GPU capacity or ephemeral GPUs? What's the cost tradeoff?
[00:02:42] Diego: Ephemeral, usually. The idea is reserved GPUs handle steady throughput; ephemeral / burst pools (cheaper spot-like ephemeral in Dedicated) accept initial traffic for latency-sensitive requests. We apply a token-based gating so expensive long-generation jobs either queue or get served by cheaper model variants. Cost isn't zero but it's lower than overprovisioning all the time.

[00:03:05] [00:03:05] Elliot: How do you avoid thundering-herd when micro-pools start?
[00:03:09] Priya: Two layers — (A) staged admission: route first X% of traffic to prewarmed cache-backed instances, then gradually shift additional traffic as KV hits stabilize; (B) small randomized jitter on evictions and start times to avoid synchronized spin-ups.
[00:03:23] Samir: Hmm, and how does quantization impact the latency during these bursts? We tried int8 and saw slightly faster p99 but sometimes worse consistency.
[00:03:33] Diego: Quantization reduces per-token compute, so steady-state throughput improves. But cold-starts can be less predictable because some kernels take different warm-up paths; for example, int8 fused kernels may have extra conversion steps for certain ops. We recommend benchmarking both latency tail and variance under load.
[00:03:53] [00:03:53] Maya: We ran a quick experiment last month: for a 4k token prompt, FP16 p99 ~ 720ms, int8 p99 ~ 640ms, but int8 99.9th had more outliers due to memory access patterns — depends on sequence length distribution and KV locality.

[00:04:15] Joan: On VPC/on-prem — our security team is nervous about ephemeral instances in VPC peering. If we use prewarmed ephemeral pools, do they live inside our subnets?
[00:04:24] Priya: Two deployment modes: Dedicated in our cloud account with instances in your subnets (VPC peering or shared VPC) or Redwood-managed prewarmed pools that you access over a private link. For full control, Dedicated inside your VPC is recommended — then ephemeral GPUs are just instances in your subnets subject to your security controls and NACLs.
[00:04:44] Samir: That helps. Another question — queueing model. We currently run a naive FIFO queue and just scale when average CPU hits threshold; it's slow. What would you recommend?
[00:04:55] Diego: Move to latency-aware admission control. One approach: implement two queues — fast-path for requests that hit KV and short expected tokens, and slow-path for long-generation jobs. Apply an M/G/1 switch approximation: derive Service time distribution empirically from request traces, compute utilization rho, and then tune maximum concurrency such that P(wait > SLO) below threshold. We can share a simple spreadsheet for that.
[00:05:19] [00:05:19] Elliot: The spreadsheet would be great — the math is where we get stuck.
[00:05:22] Maya: We'll attach the capacity-model spreadsheet. Also note we recommend using tail-safety margins: reserve ~20-30% headroom on reserved GPUs for unexpected correlated sessions, plus a capped burst queue for ephemeral instances.

[00:05:40] Joan: What's your logic for 20–30%? Is that empirical?
[00:05:43] Diego: Empirical plus queuing. In many enterprise workloads, variability is heavy-tailed; 20% covers common bursts, 30% is a safety band for heavy correlation. The exact number depends on the coefficient of variation of interarrival and service times.
[00:05:58] Priya: Also consider warm-up curves: if warm-up to target KV hit-rate takes ~90s we size ephemeral capacity to absorb initial traffic for that window. If you have a lot of short sessions, you need more ephemeral capacity but for shorter durations.

[00:06:15] Samir: Can you walk through a concrete example? Assume baseline 200 RPS, occasional session of 2000 correlated requests over 20s, average generation length 600 tokens.
[00:06:26] Diego: Sure. Baseline 200 RPS * avg token rate = X tokens/sec — simplified assume 600 tokens per request — you'll get token throughput; reserved GPUs handle baseline. For a 2000-request session over 20s that's 100 RPS extra — actually it's 100 RPS sustained for 20s but if they arrive in bursts you could see spikes higher. You compute service time per request under your quantization/kernel and then derive expected concurrency. If concurrency reaches > reserved pool capacity, ephemeral pools take initial load.
[00:06:58] [00:06:58] Elliot: In that example KV warmup — what hit-rate do you expect initially and after 60s?
[00:07:03] Priya: If the session shares prefixes with cacheable prompts, initial hit-rate maybe 10–20% then ramp to 70–80% after prefix population. If prompts are unique, you get less benefit. So content reuse matters a lot.

[00:07:18] Joan: So we should prioritize caching of few high-value prefixes?
[00:07:21] Priya: Exactly. Hot-prefix identification + prewarm is high ROI.

[00:07:30] [00:07:30] Samir: On the routing side, you mentioned fallback to cheaper model variants — how do you balance quality/regression risk?
[00:07:37] Maya: We use staged rollouts: first fallback to a slightly smaller model with a quality guard (automatic evaluation on sample prompts). If metric drift exceeds threshold, automatic fallback stop and queueing backpressure triggers. For critical flows you can pin model version to avoid fallback.

[00:07:53] Diego: Also suggest graded fallbacks: smaller model for non-critical completions, and a 'serve-but-throttle' pattern for long generation tasks (e.g., reduce max tokens or generate in shorter chunks).

[00:08:06] Elliot: Network egress and VPC — does prewarming inside our subnets add network overhead?
[00:08:11] Priya: Minimal — the prewarmed pool resides in your subnets so data doesn't traverse public. The only overhead is intra-VPC traffic. For on-prem, we deploy within your datacenter and prewarm via a controlled snapshot of model KV state.

[00:08:25] [00:08:25] Joan: Snapshot of KV state — how big are these snapshots? Do they fit in GPU memory?
[00:08:32] Diego: KV cache size depends on model and tokenization. For many LLMs it's manageable — a few GBs for common prefixes. For long context or models with large kv per token it can be tens of GB. We provide tooling to estimate per-prefix kv size. For on-prem you can pin cache shards to specific GPUs to optimize locality.

[00:08:52] Samir: Regarding autoscale latency thresholds — we currently scale on CPU load and GPU util; is there a better SLO-aligned signal?
[00:08:59] Maya: Use the p95/p99 token latency and queue length as the primary signals. Also track KV hit-rate. Autoscaler rules: scale up when p95 token latency > target for 30s AND queue length > X, scale down when sustained low utilization for N minutes. That's safer than raw CPU.

[00:09:19] [00:09:19] Elliot: Can Redwood provide a config example for those autoscaler rules?
[00:09:23] Maya: Yes — we'll include a yaml snippet in the follow-up.

[00:09:28] Priya: One subtlety — for VPC/on-prem where spin-up times are larger, we bias toward conservative capacity and longer prewarm windows. If you can't spin new GPUs in <60s, then prewarmed pools become essential.

[00:09:45] Joan: Our spin-up is ~90–120s currently.
[00:09:48] Diego: Then we'd recommend maintaining a pool sized for the 95th traffic percentile during business hours and use ephemeral only for short, rare events. Also tune the admission control to shed heavy jobs gracefully.

[00:10:02] [00:10:02] Samir: What about burst crediting — can we pre-buy burst tokens?
[00:10:06] Maya: Yes, Redwood Dedicated offers burst credits for reserved customers — you can commit to baseline and buy burst credit buckets for occasional usage. We can attach pricing options.

[00:10:17] Joan: Can you share an example SLA for reserved pools and burst behaviour?
[00:10:21] Maya: We have docs — in short: reserved pools have a latency SLA at baseline capacity; burst capacity is best-effort with defined ramp-up times and a clear throttle policy when exhausted. We'll share formal SLA language.

[00:10:35] [00:10:35] Elliot: A few quick clarifying questions from our infra team — 1) How does the KV cache persist across redeploys? 2) If we restore a snapshot, can we avoid the initial 60–90s regen period?
[00:10:47] Priya: 1) We persist cache shards on ephemeral attached block storage or in-memory + checkpointed snapshots depending on deployment. 2) Yes, snapshot restore can fast-track population — think of it as warm boot. For on-prem, snapshot restore is the preferred pattern to avoid warm-up.

[00:11:02] Diego: Note on consistency: snapshot restore requires careful versioning — ensure model weights, tokenizer, and cache keys align. Mismatches lead to misses.

[00:11:12] [00:11:12] Samir: About observability: what metrics should we add to our dashboards to support decisioning?
[00:11:18] Priya: At minimum: per-route token throughput, KV hit-rate by prefix bucket, p50/p95/p99 token latency, queue length, prewarm pool occupancy, ephemeral spin-up events, and model-fallback events. Correlate with business metrics like user-facing error rates.

[00:11:36] Maya: Also instrument request fingerprinting so you can quickly identify top-N prefixes causing load and target them for caching.

[00:11:44] [00:11:44] Joan: Ok, these are helpful. Any gotchas around quantization + VPC/private?
[00:11:50] Diego: Two main gotchas — (1) quantized artifacts must be validated against your inference hardware and kernels; some custom on-prem GPUs behave differently; (2) debugging tails is harder since kernel differences can mask issues. Keep a small FP16 runway for triage.

[00:12:06] Elliot: About the simulation you mentioned earlier — can we see the code or playbook?
[00:12:10] Priya: We'll share a lightweight simulator — basically event-driven arrival generator, service time sampling, admission control layer. It's open and parameterized by your empirical trace. We'll run it with your traces in the next step.

[00:12:20] [00:12:20] Samir: Sounds good. On security — our legal team insists on SOC2 and audit logs for any managed prewarm. Do you provide that?
[00:12:29] Maya: Yes, we support SOC2-compliant deployments for Dedicated and Redwood-managed private links with audit logging. We'll include the compliance packet in the follow-up.

[00:12:39] Joan: Last question — what's a conservative starting reserved size for us? We run ~200 RPS baseline with p95 ~350ms currently on FP16.
[00:12:47] Diego: Based on those numbers and allowing for 20–30% headroom, start with reserved capacity to handle 250 RPS at your observed service time; then add a prewarmed ephemeral pool sized for a 60–90s window that can accept ~200 additional concurrent requests. We'll run exact numbers with your traces.

[00:13:02] [00:13:02] Maya: Ok recap/timeboxing next steps: Redwood runs baseline burst sim with Lyra traces (Diego), we share capacity model and autoscaler yaml (Maya), Lyra provides trace and prompt histograms (Samir/Elliot), security packet and VPC checklist attached (Priya). We'll aim to reconvene after initial sim results.

[00:13:20] Joan: Thanks everyone.
[00:13:22] Samir: Appreciate it.
